title: The computer does not know how to start Linux
what: The computer's start-up list has no entry for Linux. It may start Windows instead, or say "no boot device".
why: This happens after a BIOS reset, a new drive, or when Windows rewrites the list. Your files are fine.
fix_summary: Add a Linux entry to the start-up list. Nothing on your drives is changed.
backup_first: A copy of the current start-up list.
undo: Delete the new entry in the firmware menu.
manual: Restart, press the boot-menu key (F12, Esc or F9) and pick Linux. Then run this check again.
notes: efibootmgr -c with the shim path of the installed distro

title: Windows starts first, not Linux
what: The start-up list puts Windows before Linux, so Linux only starts if you pick it by hand.
why: Windows updates often move themselves to the front. Nothing is broken.
fix_summary: Put Linux first in the start-up list. Windows stays in the list and in the boot menu.
backup_first: A copy of the current start-up order.
undo: Run the same fix and choose Windows first, or use the firmware menu.
manual: Open the firmware boot menu (F12, Esc or F9 at power on) and choose Linux.

title: The start-up program is missing
what: The small program that starts Linux is missing from the start-up partition, so the computer cannot start Linux.
why: An update that was interrupted, or a tool that cleaned the start-up partition, can remove it. Your files are fine.
fix_summary: Put the start-up program back and rebuild the boot menu. Needs the internet.
backup_first: A copy of the boot files and drive list.
undo: The old copy is kept in the repair backup folder.
manual: Start from the Secure Linux USB stick, choose Repair, then Computer will not start.

title: The boot menu file is missing
what: The file that lists what the computer can start (the boot menu) is missing.
why: Without it the computer may stop at a black screen with a "grub>" prompt.
fix_summary: Rebuild the boot menu from the systems that are installed. Nothing is deleted.
backup_first: A copy of the existing boot menu, if there is one.
undo: Copy the saved boot menu file back.
manual: From the rescue stick: choose Repair, then Computer will not start.

title: The computer stops at a "grub rescue" prompt
what: The first-stage start-up file points at a place that is gone, so the computer stops at a text prompt.
why: It is usually caused by moving or resizing partitions, or by an interrupted update.
fix_summary: Reinstall the start-up program and rebuild the boot menu. Needs the internet.
backup_first: A copy of the boot files and drive list.
undo: The old copy is kept in the repair backup folder.
manual: From the rescue stick choose Repair, then Computer will not start.
notes: detect from the ESP grub.cfg stub

title: No system core files were found to start
what: The folder the computer starts from has no copy of the core of Linux, so it cannot start.
why: An update may have been cut off, or the start-up partition is not connected here.
fix_summary: Download and install the core of Linux again, then rebuild what it needs to start.
backup_first: A copy of the boot files and drive list.
undo: Not needed: this only puts the missing files back.
manual: Connect to the internet and run the repair from the rescue stick.

title: A start-up helper file is missing
what: One of the installed system cores has no start-up helper file, so starting it fails.
why: The helper file is made during updates. If the update stopped half-way it can be missing.
fix_summary: Rebuild the start-up helper files for every installed system core. Takes a minute or two.
backup_first: A copy of the boot files.
undo: Not needed: this only creates missing files.
manual: From the rescue stick run: Repair, then Computer will not start.

detector: cmd:jprev~Kernel panic|VFS: Unable to mount root|not syncing
title: The last start-up crashed right after an update
what: The last time the computer started it crashed very early. The newest system core may not suit this computer.
why: New system cores sometimes fail on particular hardware. The older one usually still works.
fix_summary: Start with the previous system core by default. Nothing is deleted.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
undo: Choose the newer one again in the same menu.
manual: Restart, choose Advanced options in the boot menu and pick an older version.
notes: needs a choice of which kernel

detector: cmd:jprev~You are in emergency mode|Dependency failed for Local File Systems
title: The computer stopped in "emergency mode"
what: The last start-up stopped at a text screen called emergency mode because a drive could not be opened.
why: A drive listed at start-up was missing or damaged. Fixing the list usually gets you going again.
fix_summary: Check the list of drives, fix entries that point at missing drives, and rebuild the start-up files.
backup_first: A copy of the boot files and drive list.
undo: The old files are kept in the repair backup folder.
manual: Press Ctrl+D to try again, or run Repair, then Computer will not start.

title: The drive list points at a drive that is not there
what: The file that lists your drives mentions a drive that is not connected, which makes start-up stop and wait.
why: It happens after changing a drive, resizing partitions, or unplugging a data drive.
fix_summary: Mark the missing drive as optional, so the computer starts without it. The drive is not touched.
backup_first: A dated copy of the drive list.
undo: Copy the saved drive list back.
manual: Edit the drive list (/etc/fstab) and add "nofail" to the line of the missing drive.

title: Windows is installed but not in the boot menu
what: Windows was found on this computer, but the boot menu has no entry for it.
why: Without an entry you must use the firmware boot menu every time to start Windows.
fix_summary: Turn on the Windows finder and rebuild the boot menu. Windows is not changed.
backup_first: A copy of the boot menu settings.
undo: Run the same fix and turn the finder off in /etc/default/grub.
manual: Open the firmware boot menu and pick "Windows Boot Manager".

title: Windows may have lost its start-up files
what: A Windows partition is present but its start-up files are missing from the start-up partition.
why: Installing Linux or cloning drives can overwrite them. Windows will not start until they are restored.
fix_summary: Open the Windows helper, which can show the safest way to restore the Windows start-up files.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
undo: Not applicable.
manual: Use a Windows recovery USB: Repair your computer, then Startup Repair.
notes: cannot rebuild bootmgr from Linux reliably

title: Secure Boot is blocking the NVIDIA graphics driver
what: Your NVIDIA driver is installed but not loaded, because Secure Boot does not trust its key yet. The screen may be black or low quality.
why: Secure Boot only runs drivers that carry an approved signature. Approving the key takes one restart.
fix_summary: Ask Secure Boot to trust the driver key, using a one-time password you choose. Then restart and approve it on the blue screen.
backup_first: Nothing on your drives is changed.
undo: Remove the key later with secure-linux-mok-remove.
manual: Run: sudo secure-linux-drivers enroll-key, restart, and approve the key on the blue screen.
notes: correlation winner over module-missing, black-screen, sb-key

detector: env:secureboot && cmd:mokkey~not enrolled|is not enrolled|no key
title: Secure Boot has not approved the driver key
what: A driver signing key exists but Secure Boot has not approved it, so some drivers will not load.
why: Only approved drivers may run while Secure Boot is on, so graphics or Wi-Fi drivers can silently fail.
fix_summary: Ask Secure Boot to trust the driver key, using a one-time password you choose, then restart.
backup_first: Nothing on your drives is changed.
undo: Remove the key later with secure-linux-mok-remove.
manual: Run: sudo secure-linux-drivers enroll-key and approve the key on the blue screen after restart.

title: Screen went black or froze at the last start-up
what: At the last start-up the graphics driver or the login screen failed to start, which can give a black screen.
why: A graphics driver update that does not match the system core is the usual cause.
fix_summary: Open the safe graphics helper. It can start with basic graphics so you can get in.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
undo: The helper shows how to undo each step.
manual: Restart, press e in the boot menu, add the word nomodeset to the line starting with linux, and press Ctrl+X.

title: The computer is running in basic graphics mode
what: The computer was told to use basic, slow graphics (the word "nomodeset" is set), which is meant only for emergencies.
why: Videos, games and the desktop feel slow, and external screens may not work.
fix_summary: Remove the emergency graphics setting so the normal driver is used at the next start.
backup_first: A list of the current start-up settings.
undo: Run the safe graphics helper to put it back.
manual: Only remove it if your screen works without it; if the screen goes black again, put it back.

title: The start-up picture is getting stuck
what: The start-up animation did not finish properly at the last start-up, which can leave a frozen logo.
why: The animation sometimes clashes with the graphics driver. Turning it off only shows text while starting.
fix_summary: Turn off the start-up animation, so you see plain text while the computer starts.
backup_first: A list of the current start-up settings.
undo: Run the fix with the word "on" in the guide to turn the picture back on.
manual: Remove the word "splash" from the start-up settings.

title: The disk password screen waits for a drive that is missing
what: The list of locked drives mentions a drive that is not there, so the password screen can wait a long time or fail.
why: An old entry for a replaced drive keeps the computer waiting.
fix_summary: Nothing is changed automatically, because the file lists locked drives.
backup_first: Nothing is changed.
undo: Not applicable.
manual: Check /etc/crypttab. Remove or comment the line of the drive that no longer exists, then rebuild the start-up helper file.

title: The clock may be wrong after switching between Windows and Linux
what: Windows and Linux read the computer's clock differently, so the time can jump by hours after you switch.
why: Windows assumes the clock shows local time; Linux assumes world time. Choosing one way fixes it.
fix_summary: Tell Linux the clock shows local time, like Windows does. Only do this if your time jumps after switching.
backup_first: The current clock settings.
undo: Run: timedatectl set-local-rtc 0.
manual: Or make Windows use world time with a registry setting (RealTimeIsUniversal).

title: The start-up partition is almost full
what: The partition that holds the start-up files is {detail}% full. A new update may fail to install.
why: Old versions of the system core pile up there. A full partition can stop updates and the next start-up.
fix_summary: Remove old versions of the system core and keep the newest two. Your files are not touched.
backup_first: A list of what is removed.
undo: Old versions can be installed again from the software sources.
manual: Remove old system cores: sudo dnf remove --oldinstallonly --setopt installonly_limit=2 kernel-core

title: Many old system versions are piling up
what: {detail} versions of the system core are installed. Only the newest two or three are needed.
why: Old ones use space and slow down updates.
fix_summary: Remove the oldest versions and keep the newest two. Your files are not touched.
backup_first: A list of what is removed.
undo: Old versions can be installed again from the software sources.
manual: Remove old system cores with your package manager.

title: The small start-up partition is almost full
what: The EFI start-up partition is {detail}% full. Updates of the start-up program may fail.
why: That partition is small. Leftover files from other systems or tools can fill it.
fix_summary: Nothing is deleted automatically, because the files may belong to Windows.
backup_first: Nothing is changed.
undo: Not applicable.
manual: Look in /boot/efi/EFI for folders of systems you no longer use and remove those only.

title: Secure Boot was meant to be on but is off
what: You chose to use Secure Boot during setup, but the firmware currently has it switched off.
why: Secure Boot stops unsigned programs from starting before Linux does. Without it that protection is missing.
fix_summary: Switching it on is done in the firmware screen, not by software.
backup_first: Nothing is changed.
undo: Not applicable.
manual: Restart, open the firmware settings (F2, Del or Esc) and switch Secure Boot on.

title: Starting up takes a long time
what: The computer needs about {detail} seconds to start.
why: A slow start is usually one service waiting for something (often the network).
fix_summary: Nothing is changed automatically.
backup_first: Nothing is changed.
undo: Not applicable.
manual: Open System Settings > Startup and Shutdown and turn off programs you do not need at start-up.

title: The computer waits for the network while starting
what: Start-up waits about {detail} seconds for the network to come up before it carries on.
why: On a laptop this wait is not needed. The network connects in the background afterwards.
fix_summary: Stop start-up waiting for the network. The network still connects as normal.
backup_first: The current setting.
undo: Run: sudo systemctl enable NetworkManager-wait-online.service.
manual: Disable NetworkManager-wait-online.service.

title: The start-up partition is read-only
what: The start-up partition is set to read-only, so updates cannot change it.
why: Linux makes a partition read-only when it sees errors on it.
fix_summary: Open the disk check helper, which can repair the start-up partition safely.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
undo: The helper explains how to undo.
manual: From the rescue stick choose Check and repair a disk.
